_note: Sequenced curriculum. Body text supports [[entry-id]] links into encyclopedia.json, which open as definition cards in place. Lessons are meant to be read in order; each course states what it assumes.

courses.title: Start here
courses.summary: The question under test, the analogy behind it, and how to work with the instrument.

lessons.title: The question
lessons.body:
A sound that moves from left to right is heard at one position and then another, and the sequence is perceived as movement. This is well understood and involves no puzzle.

The question here is whether a whole field of sound can be heard as rotating when nothing inside it can be singled out and pointed at. Rotation is a global property of the field, and localizability is a local property of its parts, so the two can be manipulated and tested separately. The claim under test is that the first can occur without the second.

The standard account of [[auditory-motion]] holds that motion is inferred by comparing successive position estimates. Under that account, a field with nothing localizable in it provides no estimates to compare, and should not be heard as moving. A listener who hears the rotation anyway would be evidence that the account is incomplete.

Listening sessions here always address two questions: whether anything in the field can be pointed at, and whether the field is turning.

checkpoint.q: Why does a wide, enveloping sound not answer the question by itself?
checkpoint.a: Width and envelopment are separate qualities from rotation, and a wide sound still has a locatable centre. The claim requires global motion together with the absence of anything locally pointable.

lessons.title: The analogy that motivates it
lessons.body:
In vision the corresponding question is settled. A [[random-dot-kinematogram]] is a field of dots in which some proportion move together while the rest move randomly. Observers report the global motion and its direction well below the proportion at which any single dot can be followed. Motion there is computed by pooling across elements and belongs to the ensemble; see [[global-motion]].

Two details of the stimulus matter for carrying the analogy over. The dots move, and their coherence lies in a shared direction of travel. Individual dots are visible throughout; they are simply uninformative on their own.

The auditory counterpart used here is a ring of sources that travel together while each one is made too diffuse to locate. That configuration is called [[unison-rotation]] in this project.

The analogy has a known limit. Vision has many independently resolvable spatial channels, while hearing reconstructs space from a comparison between two ear signals, so any auditory pooling would operate on [[interaural-statistics|interaural statistics]] rather than on a spatial map.

checkpoint.q: What makes an individual dot in a kinematogram useless for judging the global motion?
checkpoint.a: Its own trajectory carries almost no information about the ensemble's direction. The auditory version aims for the same property through decorrelation.

lessons.title: What the instrument does
lessons.body:
The instrument sums a piece of audio to mono and builds a field from it: several virtual [[source|sources]] arranged in one or more [[ring|rings]] around the head, each filtered to differ from the others, each placed at an angle and distance through a head model.

Work is organised around a [[passage]], a time region of the track, which holds [[variant|variants]]: the untreated signal plus any number of treatments. Rendering produces every variant over the same span, sample aligned and matched in loudness, so a comparison between them isolates the treatment.

During playback the track runs untreated while each rendered variant runs alongside it in step. Holding a number key brings one forward and releasing returns to the untreated signal, with the change occurring mid-note.
lessons.try: The Passages panel starts with one passage and three variants: the untreated signal, a rotating ring, and the same ring held still.

checkpoint.q: Why are variants rendered over exactly the same span?
checkpoint.a: So the material is identical across conditions and any audible difference is attributable to the treatment rather than to the music.

lessons.title: Working method
lessons.body:
Comparison is more sensitive the closer together the compared sounds are in time, because memory for spatial quality fades quickly; see [[auditory-memory]]. Switching between aligned variants in the middle of a sustained note is therefore a stronger test than listening to renders in sequence.

A workable loop: choose a passage of fifteen to thirty seconds, build two or three variants that differ in one parameter, render, loop the passage, and switch between variants repeatedly.

Three habits protect the conclusions. Change one parameter per comparison, since a difference heard between variants that differ in two ways cannot be attributed to either. Compare against the right reference, which for a moving field is the same field held still; see [[matched-control]]. Record what was heard before reading the measurements.

Listen on headphones, with any operating-system spatializer disabled, since those apply a second head model on top of this one.
lessons.try: With Loop passage on, press Play, then hold and release key 1 several times.

checkpoint.q: Two variants differ in rotation rate and in source count, and one sounds more diffuse. What can be concluded?
checkpoint.a: Nothing attributable, since either parameter or their interaction could be responsible. Comparisons need a single difference.

courses.title: How we hear direction
courses.summary: The two interaural differences, the cues they support, and where they fail.

lessons.title: Two ears, two differences
lessons.body:
The ears sit on opposite sides of the head, and this produces two measurable differences between the signals at the two eardrums. A sound to the right arrives at the right ear earlier, which is the [[itd|interaural time difference]], at most roughly 0.65 ms for a human head. It also arrives louder, because the head shadows the far ear, which is the [[ild|interaural level difference]].

Both differences are zero for directions on the [[median-plane]], the vertical plane of symmetry through the head, and maximal on the [[interaural-axis]] through the ears. What the pair really encodes is the angle from that axis, a fact with consequences covered later in this course.

Hearing that rests on comparing the two ear signals is called [[binaural]].

checkpoint.q: Why are both interaural differences zero for a sound directly behind the listener?
checkpoint.a: That direction is equidistant from the two ears, as straight ahead is, so the signals match in both time and level.

lessons.title: Timing and its limits
lessons.body:
The auditory system extracts [[itd]] by comparing the fine structure of the two ear signals. Neurons phase-lock to the waveform at low frequencies, and the comparison of their timing yields the delay.

Above roughly 1.5 kHz this fails for two reasons: phase-locking to individual cycles degrades, and the wavelength becomes shorter than the head, which makes the cycle-to-cycle comparison ambiguous. The envelope of a high-frequency sound still carries usable timing, but fine-structure timing is a low-frequency mechanism.

Human resolution for interaural delay is near 10 microseconds. One sample at 44.1 kHz lasts about 23 microseconds, so a renderer that rounded delays to whole samples would be audibly coarse, and delays are instead interpolated between samples; see [[fractional-delay]].

checkpoint.q: Why does a binaural renderer need delays finer than one sample?
checkpoint.a: Interaural timing resolution is around 10 microseconds and a sample at 44.1 kHz is 23 microseconds, so sample-rounded delays would quantise the cue audibly.

lessons.title: Level and frequency
lessons.body:
The head shadows sound only when the wavelength is small relative to the head. A 100 Hz tone, with a wavelength near 3.4 m, bends around it by [[diffraction]]; an 8 kHz tone, with a wavelength near 4 cm, is blocked.

The [[ild]] is therefore a function of frequency. Measured from this instrument's model at 90° to the right: about +1.3 dB at 200 to 500 Hz, +7.8 dB at 1 to 2 kHz, and +15.2 dB at 4 to 8 kHz. A plausible head-shadow model is consequently a filter rather than a flat gain; see [[brown-duda-shadow]].

Together with the previous lesson this gives the [[duplex-theory]]: timing dominates at low frequencies and level at high ones.

One consequence recurs later. The bass carries very little level difference, so low frequencies offer almost no cue for position, and decorrelating them tends to produce vagueness rather than width; see [[bass-coherence]].
lessons.try: The crossovers and band amounts in a variant's Decorrelation group exist for the reason in the last paragraph.

checkpoint.q: Why is the interaural level difference small below a few hundred hertz?
checkpoint.a: Those wavelengths exceed the size of the head, so the sound diffracts around it rather than being shadowed, and little level difference arises.

lessons.title: The cone of confusion
lessons.body:
Since [[itd]] and [[ild]] encode the angle from the [[interaural-axis]], every direction on a cone around that axis produces the same pair of values; see [[cone-of-confusion]]. Front and back at mirror-image angles are the simplest such pair.

Listeners resolve the ambiguity in two ways. The [[pinna]] imposes direction-dependent [[spectral-cues]], mostly above 5 kHz, which differ between front and back and also carry [[elevation]]. More decisively, small head movements shift the cues in opposite directions for front and back sources; see [[head-movement-cue]]. Static headphone listening removes head movement, and the spherical model used here has no pinna.

The consequence for this instrument is complete [[front-back-confusion]]: azimuths 0° and 180° produce identical signals. A full rotation yields an interaural pattern that repeats twice per lap, so rotation cannot be distinguished from side-to-side oscillation at twice the rate, and rotation direction cannot be recovered. Listening questions about pointing remain valid; questions about direction do not, which is why the blind test does not ask one.

checkpoint.q: Which listening question remains valid despite the front-back symmetry?
checkpoint.a: Whether any individual source can be pointed at. Judgements of rotation direction are not recoverable under this model.

lessons.title: The spherical model's scope
lessons.body:
The head model is a rigid sphere of radius 8.75 cm; see [[spherical-head-model]]. From that geometry the [[woodworth-model]] yields the ITD and the [[brown-duda-shadow]] filter yields a frequency-dependent ILD, and both have been verified against the figures earlier in this course.

A sphere has no pinna, so the model produces no [[spectral-cues]], no [[elevation]], and no front-back discrimination, and it corresponds to no listener in particular; see [[individualization]]. It places sounds convincingly left and right and supports the coherence manipulations this project depends on.

The upgrade path is measured data in [[sofa]] format, for which the code already has a drop-in class. The substantive work there is [[hrtf-interpolation]], since naive blending between measured directions causes [[comb-filtering]].
lessons.try: Head radius and speed of sound appear in a variant's Physical model group and feed the formulas above directly.

checkpoint.q: What capability arrives first with measured HRTFs?
checkpoint.a: Front-back discrimination, through pinna spectral cues, which would make rotation direction answerable.

courses.title: Building a virtual field
courses.summary: Convolution, HRIRs, ring geometry, and time-varying rendering.

lessons.title: Impulse responses and convolution
lessons.body:
For a linear time-invariant system, the response to a single instantaneous impulse characterises the system completely: the output for any input follows from it. That recording is the [[impulse-response]], and the operation that applies it is [[convolution]], in which every output sample is a weighted sum of recent input samples with the impulse response supplying the weights.

Most of this instrument is expressed in impulse responses. The path from a direction to an eardrum is one, and each decorrelating filter is one.

Direct convolution costs the product of the two lengths, so in practice both signals are transformed to the frequency domain, multiplied, and transformed back, which is one reason the renderer works in blocks.

checkpoint.q: Why does the impulse response fully characterise a linear system?
checkpoint.a: Any input can be written as a sum of scaled, shifted impulses, and a linear system's response to a sum is the sum of its responses.

lessons.title: A direction as a filter
lessons.body:
The delay, shadowing, and spectral shaping a direction imposes can be collected into one filter per ear, the [[hrtf]], or in the time domain the [[hrir]]. Convolving a mono signal with a direction's pair places it in that direction over headphones.

This instrument synthesizes each pair from the model: a [[fractional-delay]] carries the [[itd]] and the [[brown-duda-shadow]] filter carries the [[ild]]. Pairs are computed for each degree of [[azimuth]] and stored. Measured data in [[sofa]] format uses the same interface, so nothing downstream changes when it is substituted.

One implementation detail is audible if done wrongly: the delay filter's window must be centred on the delay rather than on the middle of the array, since the asymmetric truncation otherwise removes high frequencies; see [[windowed-sinc]].

checkpoint.q: How are the HRTF and the HRIR related?
checkpoint.a: They are the same information in different domains, related by the Fourier transform. Rendering convolves with the time-domain form.

lessons.title: Rings of sources
lessons.body:
A field is the sum of several spatialized copies of the signal, arranged in [[ring|rings]]. Each ring sets a source count, angular positions, a rotation rate, and a distance.

Geometry interacts with symmetry. In an even ring every source has one directly opposite, and opposite pairs of identical signals cancel each other's interaural contributions; see [[antipodal-cancellation]]. Odd counts avoid exact opposition, and uneven spacing reduces the symmetry further.

Identical copies on a symmetric ring cancel completely, a result treated in the next course.
lessons.try: In a ring module, compare 4 evenly spaced sources against 5.

checkpoint.q: Why do the rings here default to odd source counts?
checkpoint.a: An even ring gives every source an exact antipode, and those pairs cancel each other's interaural contributions when the signals are identical.

lessons.title: Rendering a moving field
lessons.body:
A moving source requires a filter that changes over time, and an abrupt filter change produces a click. The renderer therefore processes short overlapping blocks, convolving each with the [[hrir]] for the angle at the block's midpoint and summing the results; see [[overlap-add]].

Blocks are tapered by a [[window-function]] that doubles as the crossfade between successive filter settings. The taper must satisfy [[cola]], the condition that overlapping windows sum to a constant, since otherwise the output is amplitude-modulated at the block rate. A periodic [[hann-window]] at half-block overlap satisfies it exactly.

The default block of 256 samples updates positions about 344 times per second, well beyond what the binaural system can track; see [[binaural-sluggishness]]. The same per-block update applies to the decorrelation amounts, which is what allows a coherence structure to move independently of the sources.

checkpoint.q: What happens when the analysis windows fail the constant-overlap condition?
checkpoint.a: The reconstruction acquires ripple at the block rate, heard as amplitude modulation.

courses.title: Coherence and decorrelation
courses.summary: Why identical copies cancel, how copies are made to differ, and what each control contributes.

lessons.title: Two coherences
lessons.body:
Two signals are coherent when one predicts the other, and incoherent when it does not, with a continuum between; see [[coherence]]. The measure used is the [[correlation-coefficient]], which is normalised so that level does not affect it.

Two distinct coherences appear throughout this instrument. Inter-source coherence holds between source signals before spatialization, is what the decorrelation controls act on, and is reported as a [[coherence-matrix]]. Interaural coherence holds between the two ear signals after summation and is measured as [[iacc]]. The two are related but move separately, and conclusions drawn about one from the other are unreliable.

checkpoint.q: Which coherence do the decorrelation controls act on directly?
checkpoint.a: Inter-source coherence. Interaural coherence at the ears is a downstream result that also depends on geometry and the head model.

lessons.title: The degenerate ring
lessons.body:
An evenly spaced ring in which every source carries the same signal renders with the left and right channels identical to machine precision. The result is a centred mono image with no interaural information, and rotating the ring changes nothing beyond a faint timbral shimmer from shifting [[comb-filtering]]. The measurement appears in the test suite; see [[degenerate-ring]].

The cancellation is a symmetry property: summing identical copies over a symmetric arrangement removes exactly the interaural differences that would carry direction. Rotation can only be audible after the symmetry is broken, through [[decorrelation]], uneven spacing, per-source gain, or per-source coherence; see [[symmetry-breaking]].

A silent-seeming result is most often this configuration, so it is the first thing to check.
lessons.try: Add the Coherent ring preset and compare its measured IACC of 1.000 against the rotating ring.

checkpoint.q: A rotating ring produces no audible motion. What is checked first?
checkpoint.a: The decorrelation amount. A coherent symmetric ring cancels to mono and carries no rotation at any rate.

lessons.title: Decorrelating without changing timbre
lessons.body:
The requirement is copies that are mutually incoherent while each still sounds like the original. Timbre follows the [[magnitude-spectrum]], so the filters must leave magnitude essentially flat while altering timing, which is the definition of [[allpass-filter|allpass]].

Two constructions are used. A random-phase allpass filter scrambles the [[phase-spectrum]] completely and preserves magnitude exactly, at the cost of smearing transients. [[velvet-noise]] places sparse random-sign impulses on a jittered grid, is nearly colourless, cheap to convolve, and gentler on transients.

The two lie on one axis: as velvet's [[impulse-density]] rises, the sequence approaches a random sign sequence, which is the allpass case. The blend between the untreated and filtered signal is the [[decorrelation-amount]].

checkpoint.q: Why must a decorrelating filter be approximately allpass?
checkpoint.a: A filter that changed the magnitude spectrum would change timbre, and comparisons would then be about colouration rather than coherence.

lessons.title: Which controls do work
lessons.body:
Measured on this system, the controls differ widely in usable range.

[[ir-length|IR length]] has the most: inter-source coherence runs from about 0.19 at 5 ms to 0.04 at 120 ms, large against the measurement [[noise-floor]] of roughly 0.05. Longer filters also smear transients more.

[[impulse-density|Density]] acts only while the filter is sparse, with coherence falling from about 0.50 at 60 impulses per second to 0.07 at 400 and remaining flat beyond; see [[density-saturation]].

[[ir-envelope|Envelope]] dominates in the sparse regime and is nearly inert once dense, and it previously confounded comparisons between the two filter families; see [[envelope-confound]]. It is held fixed when anything else is compared.

[[phase-depth|Phase depth]] provides a smooth route to partial coherence. [[micro-delay]] and [[micro-pitch]] decorrelate crudely and colour recognisably, and are kept for comparison. The [[coherence-lfo]] varies the amount over time.
lessons.try: Set envelope to flat explicitly and sweep IR length from 5 to 120 ms across renders, watching the measured coherence.

checkpoint.q: A large difference appears between velvet at 200 impulses per second and allpass. What is ruled out first?
checkpoint.a: The IR envelope, which historically differed between the two presets and dominates when the filter is sparse.

lessons.title: Level and the low end
lessons.body:
A plain blend between the untreated and filtered signal is not power preserving: the components partially cancel, and the middle of the sweep sits several decibels below the ends. Loudness differences dominate subjective comparison, so such a control would make every comparison about level. Each control here holds per-source level constant through a closed-form correction, verified per control in the test suite; see [[level-preserved]] and [[level-matching]].

Frequency receives separate treatment. The bass carries little [[ild]], so decorrelating it produces vagueness and risks partial cancellation on summing, and common practice keeps it coherent; see [[bass-coherence]]. The [[crossover]] is adjustable because that practice has not been tested on rotating fields, and the band splitting is arranged so that uniform band amounts change nothing at all.

checkpoint.q: Why is level preservation checked per control rather than once overall?
checkpoint.a: Any single control that leaked level would bias every comparison made with it, so each axis is verified separately.

courses.title: Putting a field in motion
courses.summary: Building motion from lattices and motion fields: turning, drifting, closing in, and mixtures of these.

lessons.title: Motion in unison
lessons.body:
The main configuration is a ring of mutually decorrelated sources rotating together at one rate, called [[unison-rotation]] in this project.

Its two properties come from two independent controls. The ring rate moves every source together, keeping the formation rigid. The [[decorrelation-amount]] removes each source's individual locatability. At low decorrelation the result is trackable objects circling the listener, which is unremarkable; at high decorrelation the sources merge into a diffuse field, and whether that field is still heard to turn is the experimental question.

This is the configuration corresponding to the [[random-dot-kinematogram]], with decorrelation playing the role that per-dot uninformativeness plays in vision.
lessons.try: The Monitor shows each source's trail and a rigid outline connecting the ring while it rotates.

checkpoint.q: Which control carries rotation and which carries unlocalizability?
checkpoint.a: The ring rate carries rotation and the decorrelation amount carries unlocalizability. Their independence is what makes the question testable.

lessons.title: Choosing a rate
lessons.body:
Usable rates are bounded on both sides. Below the [[mama|minimum audible movement angle]], motion traverses too little arc to register within a listening window. Above the limit set by [[binaural-sluggishness]], the binaural system's integration window of a hundred milliseconds or more smooths the changing cues into texture.

Working figures from listening here: drift near 30°/s, clear rotation between roughly 60 and 120°/s, and loss of the motion impression somewhere past a few hundred.

For measurements, note that the front-back symmetric model makes the interaural pattern repeat twice per lap, so a ring at 90°/s modulates the cues at 0.5 Hz; see [[interaural-pattern-rate]].

checkpoint.q: At 120°/s, what is the interaural pattern rate under this model?
checkpoint.a: 0.667 Hz. A lap takes three seconds and the pattern completes twice per lap.

lessons.title: Choosing material
lessons.body:
Material affects the outcome more than any parameter. Under identical treatment, sustained theremin passages reach [[iacc]] near 0.04 while guitar remains between 0.38 and 0.62; see [[transient-material]].

A transient is a sharp, precisely timed event, and such events give the auditory system discrete snapshots from which positions are fixed. Those snapshots are the localization the experiment is trying to remove, so material full of onsets works against the treatment regardless of settings.

Suitable material is sustained and nearly transient-free: pads, drones, bowed strings, organ, held voice, cymbal wash. When the percept fails to appear, the passage is worth changing before the parameters.
lessons.try: Treat a sustained section and a percussive section with identical settings and compare.

checkpoint.q: Why does percussive material resist this treatment?
checkpoint.a: Its onsets provide well-timed localization snapshots, restoring the pointable positions the configuration is designed to remove.

lessons.title: Depth, drift, and partial coherence
lessons.body:
Rings need not be single or stationary in radius. Each ring has a distance, carried by level and by the near-field growth of the [[ild]]; see [[source-distance]]. Two rings at different distances and rates make a field with depth, an inner and outer structure that can rotate together, at different speeds, or in opposite directions. The distance cue is thin without reverberation, so expectations should be modest, and the level balance between rings still audibly separates them.

A ring can also give a share of its sources to smooth random wandering instead of rotation; see [[motion-coherence]]. This transfers the kinematogram's central manipulation: in vision, the proportion of coherently moving dots sets the strength of the global motion signal, and the threshold proportion is a standard psychophysical measure. Sweeping the share here asks how much coherent motion the auditory ensemble requires before it reads as turning. Radial wander adds random in-and-out motion on top.

Wander counts as motion, so the matched control for these configurations freezes it along with the rotation, holding each wanderer at its seed-determined offset.
lessons.try: Add the Partly random motion preset and its control, or the Two rings preset, and compare against plain unison rotation.

checkpoint.q: What is the correct static control for a field with wandering sources?
checkpoint.a: The same configuration with ring rates zeroed and wander frozen, which preserves the geometry while removing all motion.

courses.title: Measuring, and testing honestly
courses.summary: What the measures show, their noise floor, the rotation confound, and blind procedure.

lessons.title: IACC and its variants
lessons.body:
[[iacc]] is the correlation between the two ear signals at the best small time lag. Values near 1 indicate a coherent, centred image and values near 0 a diffuse one. The measure comes from room acoustics, where low values accompany [[envelopment]] and [[apparent-source-width|width]].

On a static ring it tracks the decorrelation amount monotonically, from 1.000 through roughly 0.92 and 0.55 to near 0.22 at full decorrelation.

Two refinements are reported alongside it. [[octave-bands|Per-band]] values show where the coherence went, with the low bands being where decorrelation costs the most. The [[iacc-over-time]] series shows change within a passage, which a single number averages away.

The next two lessons cover the measure's limits, which matter more than its values.

checkpoint.q: What does the per-band breakdown reveal that the broadband number hides?
checkpoint.a: Which frequency regions lost coherence, particularly the low bands, where decorrelation produces vagueness rather than width.

lessons.title: The noise floor
lessons.body:
The decorrelating filters are random draws, so identical settings measure differently under different [[seed|seeds]]. Across twelve seeds at full decorrelation, [[iacc]] has a standard deviation near 0.038 and spans 0.166 to 0.283, and inter-source coherence carries about 0.05 per draw; see [[noise-floor]].

Some effects under study are smaller than this. Ring geometry moves IACC by roughly 0.04 to 0.05, which single renders cannot resolve.

The working rules follow directly: hold the seed fixed when comparing two settings, average over seeds when characterising one, and treat any difference smaller than the floor as unresolved.

checkpoint.q: Conditions measured with different seeds differ by 0.05 in IACC. What is concluded?
checkpoint.a: Nothing, since the difference is within draw-to-draw variation. The comparison needs a shared seed or averaging.

lessons.title: Measuring rotation requires a control
lessons.body:
[[iacc]] describes diffuseness and cannot distinguish a field in motion from a static one, since both can produce the same value. The alternative is to look for cyclic modulation of the [[iacc-over-time]] series at the [[interaural-pattern-rate]].

On music that measure is confounded by the material's own periodicity. Over a 20-second passage here, a fully static field scored a modulation ratio of 2.04 at 0.5 Hz while genuinely rotating fields scored 2.65 to 3.14, so the raw number cannot support a rotation claim; see [[rotation-signature]].

The interpretable quantity is the difference against a [[matched-control]]: the identical configuration, same seed, with every motion zeroed. The material's contribution then appears in both and subtracts out. The instrument pairs such controls automatically and reports the difference.

The paired figure remains noisy on short passages, having given +0.61 over 20 seconds and −0.91 over 12 for the same comparison, and a clean +4.74 on a synthetic drone with no competing periodicity. Long passages, synthetic sanity checks, and repetition across seeds are all warranted.

checkpoint.q: A rotating field scores a modulation ratio of 2.8. What does this show?
checkpoint.a: Little by itself, since a static field scored 2.04 on similar material. Only the difference against a matched control with the same seed is interpretable.

lessons.title: Disagreement between measure and ear
lessons.body:
The measures and the listening reports disagree in specific, repeatable ways. Velvet decorrelation measures slightly louder than allpass in [[lufs]] yet is reported quieter, with a much lower [[iacc]]. Ring geometry barely moves IACC in conditions where it may be plainly audible; see [[metric-vs-percept]].

These measures were developed for concert halls and steady sources and have not been validated on moving decorrelated fields, so the disagreements are informative about what the measures omit rather than errors in either direction.

The practice here is to record both, letting neither overrule the other, and to treat a heard difference that the measures deny as a result worth keeping once it survives blind testing.

checkpoint.q: The measures show two conditions as identical, but they sound different. What follows?
checkpoint.a: Both observations are recorded and the difference is tested blind. If it survives, it documents a limit of the measure.

lessons.title: Blind procedure
lessons.body:
The person who designed a stimulus knows what it should do, and that knowledge shapes perception below deliberate judgement; see [[experimenter-bias]]. The remedy is procedural rather than attitudinal.

The blind test applies four standard elements. [[blind-testing|Blinding]] hides the condition during judgement. [[randomization|Randomised order]] within each repeat prevents order effects from attaching to any condition. [[forced-choice|Fixed response formats]] make answers countable and chance performance defined. [[catch-trial|Catch trials]] with the untreated signal calibrate how much of the other responses is expectation.

The bench serves unblinded exploration, and the blind test decides whether an explored difference is real; the two have different evidential standing.

Every result so far also comes from one listener who holds the hypothesis, on a non-individualized model; see [[n-of-1]]. Responses log to disk per trial with full parameters and export to CSV, so adding listeners requires no new construction.
lessons.try: The Blind test page runs on the selected passage's variants once they are rendered.

checkpoint.q: What does a catch trial with the untreated signal measure?
checkpoint.a: The rate of reporting effects where none exist, which calibrates the listener's remaining responses against expectation.
